name: Bolandione

lead: Bolandione is a prohormone that the body converts to nandrolone. It was sold as a supplement in the US until 2005.
It is now a controlled substance and is chiefly remembered for doping-test false positives.

paras: Oral intake leads to conversion to nandrolone; its own androgen receptor activity is weaker than DHT.
US Schedule III and prohibited in sport. Animal data suggest oral routes are inefficient for muscle but may still cause side effects, per Wikipedia.

lead: Bolandione, also known as 19-norandrostenedione or estr-4-ene-3,17-dione, is a steroid that acts as a precursor of the anabolic steroid nandrolone. It was sold without prescription in the United States as a prohormone supplement until 2005.[1]

It is a US Schedule III controlled substance and is banned under the World Anti-Doping Code.[1] Trace amounts in androstenedione products produced false-positive nandrolone doping tests in the early 2000s.[1]

paras: Wikipedia reports that bolandione is readily converted to nandrolone after oral dosing, though it activates the androgen receptor about ten times less potently than DHT.[1] A 2009 animal study described oral dosing as a very ineffective way to build skeletal muscle, and a 2008 rat study found muscle-selective effects with weak androgenic activity when given subcutaneously.[1]

It was marketed over the counter as a prohormone in the US until 2005. Because it yields the same urinary metabolite as nandrolone (19-norandrosterone), a 2000 JAMA study showed that users of contaminated androstenedione supplements could test positive.[1] See also the separate entry on 19-nor-4-androstenedione.
No studies found specific to appearance or muscle outcomes in humans. Related doping-control research is covered in the entry on 19-nor-4-androstenedione.

timeline.event: JAMA study shows contaminated androstenedione supplements can cause positive nandrolone tests.[1]
Over-the-counter sales end in the US.[1]
